passage: Maria was still rinsing the tea cups at nine at night when Mr. Rastogi's voice carried down the office, calling her drawings "a child's scribbles" in front of the interns. "Sorry, sir," she said, as usual. At home, her flatmate Simran asked why she kept apologising. "He got me in," Maria said. "Nobody else would have looked at my college. I owe him." "You do owe him thanks," said Simran. "Does that include being shouted at?" Maria stirred her dal and said nothing. She slept badly. Next morning she wrote two lines in her notebook: Thankful that he opened the door. Not okay with "scribbles". She wasn't sure yet what to do with the second line, but she left it on the page.

qa.q: What did Mr. Rastogi call Maria's drawings?
Why does Maria keep excusing how Mr. Rastogi treats her?
qa.a: He got her in and she feels she owes him, so thankfulness and hurt are mixed together.

qa.q: How could Maria honour her thanks without accepting the treatment?
qa.a: She can thank him for opening the door and still calmly refuse to be shouted at, for example by asking for feedback in private.

qa.q: How does Simran see Maria's sense of owing?
qa.a: Simran agrees Maria owes thanks but questions whether that includes being shouted at.

grounding: Maria excuses her boss because he helped her get in; she starts to separate thanks for the past from acceptance of the present treatment.
